source_text: Τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν ἐκ πλείονος τῆς παρασκευῆς καὶ πραγματείας ἀπόλλυσθαι. Εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἐφόδιον πρὸς ἀδικίαν ὁ πλοῦτος, ἐλεεινὸς ὁ πλουτῶν· εἰ δὲ ὑπηρεσία πρὸς ἀρετὴν, οὐκ ἔχει χώραν ἡ βασκανία, κοινῆς τῆς ἀπ' αὐτῶν ὠφελείας ἅπασι προκειμένης· πλὴν εἰ μή τις ἄρα τῇ περιουσίᾳ τῆς πονηρίας καὶ ἑαυτῷ βασκαίνοι τῶν ἀγαθῶν. Ὅλως δὲ, ὑπερκύψας τῷ λογισμῷ τὰ ἀνθρώπινα, καὶ πρὸς τὸ ὄντως καλὸν καὶ ἐπαινετὸν ἀπιδὼν, πολλοῦ ἄν τι δέοις τῶν φθαρτῶν καὶ γηΐνων μακαριστὸν κρῖναι καὶ ζηλωτόν. Οὕτω δὲ ἔχοντι, καὶ μὴ ὡς ἐπὶ μεγάλοις ἐκπεπληγμένῳ τοῖς κοσμικοῖς, ἀμήχανόν ποτε παραγενέσθαι τὸν φθόνον, Εἰ δὲ πάντως δόξης ἐπιθυμεῖς, καὶ βούλει τῶν πολλῶν ὑπερφαίνεσθαι, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο οὐκ ἀνέχῃ δεύτερος εἶναι (ἔστι γὰρ οὖν δὴ καὶ τοῦτο πρὸς τὸ φθονεῖν ἀφορμή), σὺ δὲ ἐπὶ τὴν κτῆσιν τῆς ἀρετῆς, ὥσπερ τι ῥεῦμα, μετάθες σεαυτοῦ τὸ φιλότιμον. Μὴ γὰρ πάντως πλουτεῖν ἐκ παντὸς τρόπου βούλου, μηδὲ εὐδόκιμος εἶναι ἐκ τῶν τοῦ κόσμου πραγμάτων. Οὐ γὰρ ἐπὶ σοὶ ταῦτα· ἀλλὰ δίκαιος ἔσο, καὶ σώφρων, καὶ φρόνιμος, καὶ ἀνδρεῖος, καὶ ὑπομονητικὸς ἐν τοῖς ὑπὲρ εὐσεβείας παθήμασιν. Οὕτω γὰρ καὶ σεαυτὸν σώσεις, καὶ ἐπὶ μείζοσιν ἀγαθοῖς μείζονα ἕξεις τὴν περιφάνειαν. Ἡ μὲν γὰρ ἀρετὴ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, καὶ δυνατὴ κτηθῆναι τῷ φιλοπόνῳ· ἡ δὲ τῶν χρημάτων περιβολὴ, καὶ ὥρα σώματος, καὶ ὄγκος ἀξιωμάτων, οὐκ ἐφ' ἡμῖν. Εἰ τοίνυν καὶ μεῖζον ἀγαθὸν ἡ ἀρετὴ καὶ διαρκέστερον, καὶ ὁμολογουμένην παρὰ πάντων ἔχουσα τὴν προτίμησιν, ταύτην ἡμῖν διωκτέον· ἣν ἐγγενέσθαι τῇ ψυχῇ, ἀπό τε τῶν ἄλλων παθῶν καὶ μάλιστα δὴ πάντων ἀπὸ τῆς βασκανίας μὴ καθαρευούσῃ, ἀμήχανον. Οὐχ ὁρᾷς ἡλίκον κακὸν ἡ ὑπόκρισις; Καὶ αὕτη καρπός ἐστι τοῦ φθόνου. Τὸ γὰρ διπλοῦν τοῦ ἤθους ἐκ φθόνου μάλιστα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἐγγίνεται, ὅταν, τὸ μῖσος ἐν τῷ βάθει κατέχοντες, ἀγάπῃ δεικνύωσι κατακεχρωσμένην τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν· κατὰ τὰς ὑφάλους πέτρας, αἳ, βραχεῖ ὕδατι καλυπτόμεναι, κακὸν ἀπροόρατον τοῖς ἀφυλάκτοις γίνονται. Εἰ τοίνυν καὶ θάνατος ἡμῖν ἐκεῖθεν ὥσπερ ἐκ πηγῆς ἐπεῤῥύη, ἀγαθῶν ἔκπτωσις, Θεοῦ ἀλλοτρίωσις, θεσμῶν σύγχυσις, καὶ ἀνατροπὴ πάντων ὁμοῦ τῶν κα-τὰ τὸν βίον καλῶν· πεισθῶμεν τῷ Ἀποστόλῳ, καὶ Μὴ γενώμεθα κενόδοξοι, ἀλλήλους προκαλούμενοι, ἀλλήλοις φθονοῦντες· ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον χρηστοὶ, εὔσπλαγχνοι, χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς, ὡς καὶ ὁ Θεὸς ἐχαρίσατο ἡμῖν, ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ Κυρίῳ ἡμῶν, μεθ' οὗ ἡ δόξα τῷ Πατρὶ σὺν τῷ ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.
thought_title: Virtue is the only true object of ambition
orientation: Basil is concluding his homily by showing that the remedy for envy is to transfer one's ambition from worldly goods to virtue, which is within our power, and he ends by quoting the Apostle Paul's exhortation to kindness.
pass_a_gloss: For this is to be destroyed from greater preparation and effort. For if wealth is a provision for injustice, the rich man is pitiable; but if it is a service for virtue, envy has no place, since the benefit from these things is set before all as common; unless perhaps someone by the abundance of wickedness envies himself of good things. And in general, having looked over human things with reasoning, and having looked away to the truly beautiful and praiseworthy, you would need much to judge any of the corruptible and earthly things blessed and enviable. And for the one who is so disposed, and not struck with amazement at worldly things as at great things, it is impossible that envy ever come to be present. But if you altogether desire glory, and you wish to appear above the many, and because of this you do not endure to be second (for this too is indeed a starting point for envying), do you transfer your love of honor to the acquisition of virtue, like some stream. For do not altogether wish to be rich in every way, nor to be esteemed from the affairs of the world. For these things are not in your power; but be just, and temperate, and prudent, and courageous, and patient in sufferings for piety. For thus you will both save yourself, and for greater goods you will have greater distinction. For virtue is in our power, and able to be acquired by the lover of labor; but the possession of money, and bloom of body, and bulk of dignities, are not in our power. If therefore virtue is both a greater good and more lasting, and has the preference agreed by all, this we must pursue; which to come to be in the soul that is not pure from the other passions and especially from envy above all, is impossible. Do you not see how great an evil hypocrisy is? And this is a fruit of envy. For the doubleness of character comes to be in humans especially from envy, whenever, holding the hatred in the depth, they display the surface colored over with love; like the underwater rocks, which, covered by a little water, become an unforeseen evil to the unwary. If therefore death flowed to us from there as from a spring, loss of good things, estrangement from God, confusion of laws, and overturning of all the beautiful things in life at once; let us obey the Apostle, and let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another; but rather kind, tender-hearted, forgiving one another, as also God forgave us, in Christ Jesus our Lord, with whom is the glory to the Father with the Holy Spirit unto the ages of ages. Amen.

lemmas.gloss: having looked over, having risen above
having looked away to, having regarded
to appear above, to be conspicuous above

choices.why: The optative with ἄν expresses a strong necessity or requirement, not a mild 'hardly'; the idiom δέω with genitive means 'to lack, to need', so the sense is 'you would be far from' or 'you would need much to'.
rejected: you would be far from judging

choices.english: having looked over human things with reasoning
choices.why: The aorist participle with dative of instrument expresses the act of rising above human affairs by means of rational thought; 'looked over' preserves the spatial metaphor of the compound verb.
rejected: having transcended human things in thought
having risen above human things by reason

choices.why: The perfect passive participle of καταχρώννυμι means 'painted over, colored over'; 'colored over' preserves the metaphor of a deceptive outer coating hiding the hatred beneath.
The adjective ὕφαλος means 'under the sea, submerged'; 'underwater rocks' is the natural English equivalent for the hidden danger Basil compares to the envious person's concealed hatred.
ἔκπτωσις means 'falling out, loss, deprivation'; 'loss of good things' captures the sense of being deprived of goods as a consequence of envy.
σύγχυσις means 'confusion, confounding'; 'confusion of laws' preserves the sense that envy overturns the established order of divine and human ordinances.

bible_refs.note: Μὴ γενώμεθα κενόδοξοι, ἀλλήλους προκαλούμενοι, ἀλλήλοις φθονοῦντες

pass_b_english: For this is to be destroyed from a greater supply and effort. If wealth is a provision for injustice, the rich man is pitiable; but if it is a service for virtue, envy has no place, since the benefit from these things lies open to all in common—unless, perhaps, by the excess of his wickedness a man envies himself his own good things. In general, when you have looked over human things with your reasoning and fixed your gaze on what is truly beautiful and praiseworthy, you would be far from judging any corruptible and earthly thing blessed and enviable. And for the one who is in this state, and is not struck with awe at worldly things as if they were great, it is impossible for envy ever to come near.

But if you absolutely desire glory, and you wish to be conspicuous above the many, and for this reason you cannot bear to be second—for this too is indeed an occasion for envying—then transfer your love of honor, like some stream, to the acquisition of virtue. Do not absolutely wish to be rich by every means, nor to be esteemed from the affairs of the world. For these things are not in your power. But be just, and self-controlled, and prudent, and courageous, and patient in sufferings endured for piety. For in this way you will both save yourself, and for greater good things you will have greater distinction. For virtue is in our power, and can be acquired by the one who loves labor; but the possession of money, and bodily beauty, and the weight of dignities, are not in our power.

If, then, virtue is both a greater good and more lasting, and has the acknowledged preference from all, this is what we must pursue. And it is impossible for it to be born in a soul that is not clean from the other passions, and most of all from envy. Do you not see how great an evil hypocrisy is? This too is a fruit of envy. For the doubleness of character comes to human beings especially from envy, when, holding hatred in the depths, they display a surface colored over with love—like rocks in shallow water, which, covered by shallow water, become an unseen evil for the unwary.

If, then, death has flowed to us from there as from a spring, and loss of good things, and estrangement from God, and confusion of laws, and the overturning of all the beautiful things of life together, let us obey the Apostle, and let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another (Galatians 5:26); but rather let us be kind, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as also God forgave us—in Christ Jesus our Lord, with whom be glory to the Father with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

problems.quote: forgiving one another, as also God in Christ forgave us
problems.source_quote: χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς, ὡς καὶ ὁ Θεὸς ἐχαρίσατο ἡμῖν
problems.why: Source says 'forgiving yourselves' (ἑαυτοῖς), not 'one another'; changes the command from mutual self-forgiveness to interpersonal forgiveness.
problems.fix: forgiving yourselves, as also God forgave us
problems.ruling: ἑαυτοῖς is reflexive 'yourselves,' not reciprocal 'one another'; command is self-forgiveness, not mutual.

problems.quote: as also God in Christ forgave us
problems.source_quote: ὡς καὶ ὁ Θεὸς ἐχαρίσατο ἡμῖν
problems.why: 'in Christ' is not in this clause; it belongs to the doxology 'ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ Κυρίῳ ἡμῶν'. Adds words to the quotation.
problems.ruling: ἐν Χριστῷ belongs to doxology, not forgiveness clause; 'in Christ' falsely inserted into quotation.

edits.old: forgiving one another, as also God in Christ forgave us
edits.new: forgiving yourselves, as also God forgave us

fixed: Changed 'forgiving one another, as also God in Christ forgave us' to 'forgiving yourselves, as also God forgave us': source has 'ἑαυτοῖς' (yourselves), not 'one another', and 'in Christ' is not in this clause but belongs to the doxology.

problems.why: ἑαυτοῖς is dative plural 'to one another,' not 'yourselves.'

fixed: Changed 'forgiving yourselves' to 'forgiving one another' because the source 'χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς' uses the dative plural reciprocal pronoun, meaning 'to one another,' not 'yourselves.'

problems.quote: like underwater rocks, which, covered by a little water
problems.source_quote: κατὰ τὰς ὑφάλους πέτρας, αἳ, βραχεῖ ὕδατι καλύπτονται
problems.why: βραχεῖ ὕδατι means 'shallow water,' not 'a little water'; the danger is shallows, not quantity.
problems.fix: like rocks in shallow water, which, covered by shallow water
problems.ruling: βραχεῖ ὕδατι is 'shallow water' (βραχύς = short/shallow), not 'a little water'; the danger is hidden shallows.

problems.why: ἀπροόρατον means 'unseen' or 'invisible,' not 'unforeseen'; the rocks cannot be seen through the water.
problems.ruling: ἀπροόρατον means 'unseen/invisible' (from προοράω 'to see beforehand/see'), not 'unforeseen'; rocks hidden from sight.

problems.quote: you would need much before you judged any corruptible and earthly thing blessed and enviable
problems.source_quote: πολλοῦ ἄν τι δέοις τῶν φθαρτῶν καὶ γηΐνων μακαριστὸν κρῖναι καὶ ζηλωτόν
problems.why: Misreads πολλοῦ δέοις ('you would be far from') as needing much; means 'you would be far from judging...'
problems.fix: you would be far from judging any corruptible and earthly thing blessed and enviable
problems.ruling: πολλοῦ δέοις = 'you would be far from'; 'you would need much before' changes meaning and misleads reader.

dismissed.why: 'ἔκπτωσις' means 'falling away from/loss of status,' stronger than 'loss'
dismissed.note: 'Loss of good things' fairly renders ἀγαθῶν ἔκπτωσις; the requested change is only stylistic.
